Stated Claim / Post Context:
Sean Duffy and the Perils of Trump’s Made-for-TV Cabinet

The secretary of transportation was a reality-TV “star” and a Fox Business cable host. But when the American aviation system was grounded, he lost it.

Actual Article Body:

New to The Nation? Subscribe

Print subscriber? Activate your online access

The secretary of transportation was a reality-TV “star” and a Fox Business cable host. But when the American aviation system was grounded, he lost it.

Twenty years ago, Sean Duffy was a washed-up reality-TV personality competing in lumberjack contests and making ends meet as a small-town district attorney in northern Wisconsin. Then, the 2010 Tea Party election wave swept him into Congress. But Duffy wasn’t exactly satisfied with the new gig. He grumbled about the pay—$174,000 annually—and, in 2019, he quit to become a lobbyist and the cohost of a cable show on the Fox Business channel.

This turned out to be an unexpectedly shrewd choice. Duffy was glib, good-looking, and on cable news, and that was enough to convince Donald Trump—who, as we all know, thinks that being glib, good-looking, and on cable news automatically qualifies you to run essential sections of the federal government—to nominate the Wisconsinite as the nation’s 20th secretary of transportation. Unfortunately, like so many of the score of Fox hosts who have gotten Trump administration gigs as cabinet secretaries, czars, ambassadors, and Justice Department hangers-on, Duffy was woefully unprepared to do the job.

That was abundantly clear last Friday, when Duffy was called upon to explain the FAA’s decision to bring the nation’s aviation system to a halt. In the same week that another Fox alum, “War Secretary” Pete Hegseth, narrowly escaped impeachment, Duffy was thrust into the limelight as a bumbling sidekick for Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, himself a former mixed martial arts prizefighter. At a moment of national anxiety, Duffy defaulted to the talking-head formula, which imagines that any crisis—no matter how serious—can be addressed with a word salad of implication, insinuation and invective.

Duffy’s performance was so miserable that it provoked an immediate demand for his removal from New York Governor Kathy Hochul, who called to mind the cabinet secretary’s former career as a “star” of MTV’s The Real World: Boston and his recently launched reality travel series The Great American Road Trip. “Through it all, he’s been more focused on starring in his own reality show than addressing the crisis at his agency,” said Hochul, adding, “From chronic air traffic controller shortages to repeated communications breakdowns, serious lapses in our aviation system...
